You pass if you named all four bugs and their tools. Getting the bugs right but not the tools is a partial pass, and missing a bug is a fail.

Undefined behaviour is what the C++ standard leaves unsaid about what a program does next, and it lets the compiler assume the behaviour never happens at all. Signed overflow is one example. A check like
about to wrap, compiles away, because the compiler may assume

never overflows and folds the comparison to false. Most undefined behaviour you meet day to day is one of five memory bugs: reading memory after it's freed or after its scope ends, reading or writing past the end of a buffer, freeing the same pointer twice, reading a variable nobody set, and an owner that never releases what it holds, which is a leak.
The problem is that none of this shows up as a compile error and often not even as a wrong answer. A
that reallocates frees its old block silently, so a reference taken before the
reads freed memory afterwards and, without a sanitizer, may still print a plausible number.

The tools name what the language leaves silent. AddressSanitizer catches a use after free, a double free and most out-of-bounds accesses at the moment they happen, and it prints which region was touched and where it was allocated and freed. UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer catches the arithmetic and pointer mistakes, such as the overflow above, that stay silent even under AddressSanitizer. Both are compiler flags:
. GDB steps through a program that already crashed or is misbehaving:
show or trap a value changing.

What the sanitizers cost you is a false sense of coverage: they only report the line that actually ran, so a bug on a path no test takes stays invisible, and reading uninitialised memory is one that GCC's own sanitizers mostly miss.

You meet this in the robot itself: a lambda that captures a counter by reference, the shape callbacks take in event-driven and ROS code, can quietly rewire a write meant for a trip counter onto a battery reading, and only a watchpoint finds it, because a search for the field's name finds nothing. It is also the shape of the interview question on this page: naming the bug and the tool that would catch it from a plain reading of ten lines of code.

That is the practical meaning of undefined behaviour. The standard places no requirements on a program that does it (

), and compilers use that freedom to optimise. A valid program never overflows a signed integer, never reads past the end of an array and never dereferences a null pointer, so the compiler takes those as facts: it deletes checks that could only fire after undefined behaviour, reorders code, and assumes pointers are valid. Neither GCC sanitizer tracks whether memory has been initialised. Valgrind's Memcheck does, and its manual says a program runs 20 to 30 times slower under it (
). Clang's MemorySanitizer does it at a typical slowdown of 3 times, but GCC doesn't offer it, and it needs all the code the program runs built with it, even the C library (
). The cheapest defence is to give every variable a value where you declare it, here
C++26 changes the rule for this case. Reading an uninitialised local variable becomes
: the variable holds a fixed value that the implementation chooses, compilers are encouraged to diagnose the read, and the optimiser may no longer assume the read can't happen (
A conversion that loses data is a different gap. Like the
trap in exercise 3, it is defined behaviour, so UBSan has nothing to report, and the result is wrong without any error.
A data race is invisible to AddressSanitizer and UBSan too. ThreadSanitizer finds races, but GCC's documentation says it can't be combined with
, so it needs its own build with

Every sanitizer checks only the code that runs. A use-after-free in an error path that no test takes stays hidden until a user takes it. Sanitizers make your tests stronger, and they find nothing in code that no test reaches.
